analysis.one_liner: Makes illegal robocalling and scam calling a crime, with prison time for repeat and large-scale violators.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from November 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to willfully and knowingly break the rules against unwanted robocalls and texts — punishable by up to a year in prison, or up to three years for repeat offenders, massive operations, calls meant to further a felony, or scams costing victims $5,000 or more [S2]. It would also double the fine for knowingly providing false caller ID information, from $10,000 to $20,000 [S2]. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved again [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a phone, especially the people scam robocalls hit hardest — older Americans and other targets of fraud calls that use fake caller ID to look local or official. The bill would give federal prosecutors a way to charge the people behind large-scale illegal call operations with a crime, not just hit them with civil fines they can treat as a cost of doing business, and it would make calls used to run a felony or costing victims $5,000 or more eligible for the harshest penalties [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Phone users targeted by scam robocalls

how_it_helps.text: Makes willful and knowing violations of the Telephone Consumer Protection Act a federal crime: up to 1 year in prison, and up to 3 years for repeat offenders, operations sending over 100,000 calls a day (or 10 million a year), calls intended to further a felony, or schemes costing victims $5,000 or more.

Doubles the penalty for knowingly transmitting inaccurate caller ID information from $10,000 to $20,000, targeting spoofing — the practice of making a scam call look like it comes from a local number or a government agency.
Adds 'message' and text-like communications to the definition of a call, so criminal penalties cover illegal texting as well as voice calls.

analysis.who_pays: People and companies that illegally place mass robocalls or spoof caller ID: they would face federal prosecution, prison time, and doubled civil penalties. Taxpayers would fund the additional criminal enforcement. Law-abiding telemarketers who follow consent and calling-time rules would not be affected, since the criminal provision applies only to willful and knowing violations [S2].

drawbacks.text: Criminal penalties act after the fact. Many large-scale scam operations run from overseas or through hard-to-trace networks, and prosecuting them is difficult even with a crime on the books — so the bill may deter less than its penalties suggest.

The bill only ratchets up penalties under the existing do-not-call framework; it does not add new tools like carrier-level call blocking requirements or funding for enforcement, so the underlying volume of unwanted calls could continue largely unchanged.

Any new criminal exposure carries a risk of sweeping in borderline cases. The willful-and-knowing requirement limits this, but businesses operating near the edges of the consent and disclosure rules would face a new category of legal risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted escalation aimed at behavior nearly everyone agrees is abusive — mass illegal robocalls and caller-ID spoofing used in fraud — and its carve-outs (willful and knowing intent, high-volume thresholds, repeat offenders) mean legitimate callers have little to fear. Its main limitation is design, not fairness: penalties alone do little against offshore scam operations, and the bill pairs no new enforcement resources with the new crimes. On balance, the benefit to consumers outweighs the cost, which falls on operators breaking the law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cortez Masto introduced the bill on November 15, 2023, joined by Senators Hassan, Klobuchar, and Gillibrand.

The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — the routine first step that sends a bill to the committee with jurisdiction over it.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action. The bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Illegal robocall operators and telemarketers that violate the rules are better off, because the threat of criminal prosecution never materialized. Consumers gained nothing; scam calls and spoofing remain subject only to the pre-existing civil penalty regime.

for.name: Maggie Hassan, Amy Klobuchar, and Kirsten Gillibrand
3 of 48 Senate Democrats plus 1 of 4 Senate Independents

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair: Maria Cantwell, D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship was Democratic or Independent, but no vote was ever taken and no opposition was recorded, so the partisan shape of the fight cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill would expose operators that willfully and knowingly violate calling rules to federal prison time — up to three years for repeat or high-volume offenders — and double caller-ID spoofing penalties. Legitimate callers following consent rules would be unaffected, since the crime requires willful and knowing violation.

industries.industry: Lead generation and debt-collection calling firms
industries.note: Firms that stay within the law lose nothing, but firms that aggressively skirt consent and disclosure rules would face criminal rather than merely civil exposure, raising the stakes of borderline practices.
